front_blocks.md: Define **unsaturated** (as used for hydrocarbons).

back_blocks.md: An **unsaturated** hydrocarbon contains at least one **carbon-carbon double bond** (C=C). **Alkenes** are unsaturated because they contain a C=C bond.

front_blocks.md: What is the general formula of the alkenes?

back_blocks.md: The general formula of the alkenes is C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>. This means for every n carbon atoms, there are 2n hydrogen atoms.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Alkenes are saturated hydrocarbons.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Alkenes are **unsaturated** hydrocarbons. They contain a **carbon-carbon double bond** (C=C), which means they are not fully saturated with hydrogen.

front_blocks.md: What is the functional group of the alkenes?

back_blocks.md: The functional group of the alkenes is the **carbon-carbon double bond** (C=C). This group determines the chemical reactions that alkenes undergo.

front_blocks.md: Why are alkenes more reactive than alkanes?

back_blocks.md: Alkenes are more reactive because they contain a **carbon-carbon double bond** (C=C). This double bond can break open, allowing other atoms to bond to the carbon atoms.

front_blocks.md: What do the numbers in alkene names (such as but-1-ene or pent-2-ene) indicate?

back_blocks.md: The numbers indicate the **position of the C=C double bond** — specifically, which carbon atom the double bond begins on, counting from the left of the carbon chain.

front_blocks.md: What is an **addition reaction**?

back_blocks.md: An **addition reaction** is one in which atoms of a simple molecule **add across** a double bond, converting it to a single bond. No atoms are lost in the process.

front_blocks.md: What is formed when bromine reacts with ethene?

back_blocks.md: When bromine reacts with ethene, **dibromoethane** is formed. This is an example of an **addition reaction** in which bromine atoms add across the C=C double bond.

The reaction between bromine and an alkene is a substitution reaction.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The reaction between bromine and an alkene is an **addition reaction**. Bromine atoms add across the **C=C double bond** — no atoms are removed.

front_blocks.md: Why does bromine water decolourise when added to an alkene?

back_blocks.md: Bromine water decolourises because the **bromine** atoms add across the **C=C double bond** in an addition reaction. The bromine is no longer free in solution, so the orange colour disappears.

front_blocks.md: Why is bromine water used instead of bromine in the alkene test?

back_blocks.md: Bromine water is used instead of pure **bromine** because it is **safer and easier to handle**. It still contains bromine, which reacts with alkenes in the same way.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Adding bromine water to an alkene causes the orange colour to disappear.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Alkenes react with bromine water in an **addition reaction**. The **bromine** adds across the C=C double bond, leaving no free bromine in solution, so the colour is lost.

front_blocks.md: What happens when bromine water is added to an alkane?

back_blocks.md: When bromine water is added to an **alkane**, the solution remains **orange**. Alkanes are saturated and cannot react with bromine, so the bromine stays in solution.
